patient.name: Fatima Begum
patient.complaint: Sneezing, runny nose and itchy eyes every summer, now an itchy rash on both hands at work
background: Healthcare assistant at the Royal London; wears gloves all shift
Eczema as a child; mild asthma (salbutamol as needed)
Cow's milk allergy as a baby, outgrown by age 3

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an atopic patient and symptoms soon after a trigger (urticaria, rhinitis, angioedema), or an infant with symptoms after formula; the key is IgE (immediate) versus non-IgE or Type IV (delayed).

points: Fatima, 24: every May to July, **sneezing** fits and a streaming nose.
Eyes **red, itchy and watery**; worse on park days.
Blocked nose wakes her at night.
No fever; symptoms start within minutes outdoors.

visual.title: Fatima's year: grass pollen vs symptoms
visual.caption: Symptoms rise and fall with the grass pollen season: a seasonal, allergen-driven pattern.

steps.lead: Fatima's summer symptoms are an **IgE-mediated** reaction to a harmless allergen, most likely grass pollen.
Eczema, asthma, a past milk allergy and a mother with hay fever: Fatima is **atopic** with a strong family history.
**Rhinorrhoea**, sneezing and **conjunctival redness** soon after exposure: allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Her IgE may be raised, but the history is what matters.

points: New: **itchy, red, cracked skin** on both hands and wrists.
Exactly where her **latex gloves** sit; started 3 months into the job.
Appears a day or two after long shifts, not within minutes.
No lip swelling, wheeze or faintness.

steps.q: Fatima's glove rash appears 1 to 2 days after exposure. Which reaction type is this?
steps.r: A delayed rash at the contact site is **allergic contact dermatitis**, a **Type IV** T-cell reaction. Immediate hives or wheeze would be Type I.

steps.lead: Fatima's own infant **cow's milk allergy**, outgrown by 3, fits the non-IgE pattern; her glove rash points to **patch testing** for contact dermatitis.
Fatima's poorly controlled hay fever can **worsen her asthma**; any systemic reaction raises the risk of **anaphylaxis**.

steps.text: Hives plus wheeze, stridor or low BP is not 'just an allergy': airway, breathing or circulation compromise means **anaphylaxis**, and IM adrenaline.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?': skin prick or specific IgE (RAST) for immediate allergy, skin patch testing for contact dermatitis, and mast cell tryptase to confirm anaphylaxis.

steps.lead: Fatima's history plus **skin prick testing** (grass pollen, tree pollen, house dust mite, with water and histamine controls) confirms her rhinitis trigger.

visual.title: Skin prick wheal: grass pollen
bands: Positive (3 mm or more above the water control)
visual.label: Fatima 8 mm
visual.caption: Water control 0 mm and histamine control 5 mm, so the test is valid and the grass wheal is clearly positive.

steps.title: Allergy bloods
steps.text: Grass-specific IgE is high; latex-specific IgE is negative, so her glove rash is not an IgE latex allergy.

steps.lead: **RAST** (specific IgE) backs up Fatima's grass allergy. Her eczema and asthma mean low-level positives must be read with caution.

steps.text: A positive RAST or skin prick only shows **sensitisation**. In atopic patients it can be a **false positive**: always match it to the history.

steps.lead: Fatima's hand rash needs **skin patch testing**, read at **2 to 3 days**; if she ever had anaphylaxis, **mast cell tryptase** would confirm it.

steps.title: Which allergy test?
nodes: Immediate symptoms (minutes) → skin prick or specific IgE
Delayed contact rash (days) → skin patch test
Delayed food symptoms (non-IgE) → elimination then reintroduction

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' with the allergic rhinitis ladder (oral loratadine, then intranasal steroid, then combination spray), oral antihistamines for urticaria, IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis and extensively hydrolysed formula for CMPA.

steps.q: Fatima's rhinitis now disturbs her sleep and work. Which is most appropriate initially?
o: Oxymetazoline nasal spray for a month
steps.r: Moderate to severe rhinitis (affecting sleep or activities) starts with an **intranasal corticosteroid**. Oral loratadine is first line only for mild symptoms.

steps.lead: Fatima avoids triggers (windows closed on high pollen days, swap to **nitrile gloves**). Had her rhinitis been **mild**, **oral loratadine** alone would be first line.
Her symptoms affect sleep, so she starts **intranasal mometasone**; if not controlled after 2 to 4 weeks, she switches to **fluticasone-azelastine**.

steps.title: Allergic rhinitis ladder
nodes: Still symptomatic after 2 to 4 weeks: intranasal steroid + antihistamine (fluticasone-azelastine)

visual.title: Fatima's nasal symptom score
visual.caption: Partial response at 4 weeks, so she moves to the combination spray.

steps.text: Fatima asks for **oxymetazoline** to unblock her nose. Long-term use causes **tachyphylaxis** and **rhinitis medicamentosa**: a few days at most.

steps.lead: Fatima's asthma continues on inhalers, her rhinitis on antihistamine and nasal steroid. Had her milk allergy been today, formula-fed, she would get **extensively hydrolysed formula**.
If a reaction ever becomes systemic with airway, breathing or circulation problems, Fatima needs **IM adrenaline**, repeated after **5 minutes** with an IV fluid bolus if no response.
Food allergy in children follows **NICE CG116**; milk allergy in infants follows **iMAP** and its **milk ladder**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the hypersensitivity type (I versus IV), which mediator or cell causes a symptom, why patch tests take days, or why decongestant sprays cause rebound.

steps.lead: Fatima was **sensitised** to grass pollen; each summer the pollen **cross-links** IgE on her mast cells, which then degranulate.

steps.title: Type I hypersensitivity
nodes: IgE binds Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils
Vasodilation, leak, smooth muscle contraction, mucus

steps.lead: Histamine-driven **vasodilation** and **permeability** give Fatima her runny nose and red eyes; smooth muscle contraction tightens her asthmatic airways.
Her skin prick wheal appears in 15 minutes (**IgE wheal-and-flare**); her glove dermatitis takes days because it is **Type IV** T-cell mediated.

steps.q: Fatima's childhood milk allergy had negative skin prick and RAST tests. Why?
steps.r: **Non-IgE** food allergy is **T-cell mediated**, so IgE tests are negative and diagnosis needs elimination then reintroduction.

steps.lead: Delayed, **T-cell-mediated** milk allergy explains Fatima's negative tests as a baby and why diagnosis was by **elimination and reintroduction**.
Oxymetazoline is an **alpha-agonist**; used for weeks it **downregulates receptors**, so the nose rebounds blocked when it wears off.

mcq.r: **IgE-mediated mast cell** activation and histamine release (Type I).

mcq.q: Which is a major risk factor for allergic disorders?
mcq.r: **Atopy** (eczema, asthma, hay fever) and family history.

mcq.q: By what age do most infants with non-IgE cow's milk allergy become tolerant?
mcq.r: Most non-IgE cases are tolerant by **3 years**, earlier than IgE-mediated allergy.

mcq.q: How is allergic contact dermatitis to latex or cosmetics diagnosed?
mcq.r: **Skin patch testing**, read after **2 to 3 days**.

mcq.q: What can cause a false positive RAST?
First-line treatment for mild allergic rhinitis not affecting sleep?
Moderate to severe rhinitis persists after 2 to 4 weeks of intranasal steroid. Next?
mcq.r: Switch to a combination **intranasal steroid plus antihistamine**.

mcq.q: Which formula is tried first in mild to moderate formula-fed CMPA?
Which hypersensitivity type is allergic contact dermatitis?
mcq.r: **Type IV**, delayed T-cell mediated, hence the 2 to 3 day patch test.

mcq.q: Why does prolonged oxymetazoline cause rebound congestion?

technique.stem: A 19 year old man has had sneezing, a runny, itchy nose and red, watery eyes every June and July for 3 years. Symptoms are worse after playing football in the park. He had eczema as a child. He has no fever. Examination shows pale, swollen nasal mucosa and red conjunctivae.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: is this infection, structural or allergic?

clues: worse after playing football in the park
steps.x: Seasonal, outdoor-triggered, atopic, afebrile, with eye involvement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Seasonal **allergic rhinitis** (hay fever) to grass pollen.

elim: Follows a cold, with facial pain, purulent discharge and often fever.
Persistent blockage and loss of smell, not seasonal sneezing.
Needs prolonged decongestant spray use.
Would not recur each summer with sneezing.

steps.x: **B. Allergic rhinitis.** Rule: seasonal + atopy + itch + sneezing = allergic rhinitis.

technique.stem: A 32 year old hairdresser has a 4 month history of an itchy, red, scaly rash on both hands. It flares 1 to 2 days after she uses a new hair dye at work and improves on holiday. She has no lip swelling, wheeze or urticaria.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation: first decide the type of allergy.

clues: no lip swelling, wheeze or urticaria
steps.x: Delayed rash at the site of contact with a chemical that settles away from work: allergic contact dermatitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Skin patch testing**, read after 2 to 3 days.

elim: Confirms anaphylaxis, not a contact rash.
Not needed to identify the allergen.
Tests immediate IgE allergy, not delayed Type IV.
Non-specific and does not identify a contact allergen.

steps.x: **C. Skin patch testing.** Rule: delayed contact rash = Type IV = patch test.

technique.stem: A 27 year old woman has seasonal allergic rhinitis. Her sneezing and blocked nose wake her most nights and she has missed work. She has taken oral cetirizine for 2 weeks with little benefit. Examination shows swollen nasal mucosa.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: Management: judge the severity first.
Moderate to severe allergic rhinitis (sleep and work affected), not controlled by an antihistamine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An **intranasal corticosteroid** such as mometasone or fluticasone.

elim: Not the next step for rhinitis in UK practice.
Reserved for severe, short-term rescue, not routine control.
Risks rhinitis medicamentosa; short-term only.
Considered only after optimal drug treatment fails.

steps.x: **A. Intranasal mometasone.** Rule: symptoms affecting sleep or activities = intranasal steroid.

technique.stem: A 22 year old woman has a skin prick test for suspected cat allergy. Within 15 minutes a raised, itchy wheal surrounded by redness appears at the cat dander site. The water control is negative and the histamine control positive.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this reaction?
o: Allergen cross-linking IgE on mast cells

steps.x: Mechanism: the timing tells you the hypersensitivity type.
Immediate wheal-and-flare reaction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Type I**: allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, which release histamine.

elim: Type II, e.g. haemolytic transfusion reactions.
Not the mechanism of a wheal and flare.
Type III, e.g. serum sickness, over days.
Type IV, takes 2 to 3 days (patch test).

steps.x: **A. Allergen cross-linking IgE on mast cells.** Rule: minutes = IgE/mast cell (Type I); days = T cell (Type IV).

practice.stem: A 23 year old man has had sneezing, nasal itch and a clear runny nose every spring for 4 years, with itchy, watery eyes. He has asthma. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 120/74 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Nasal mucosa is pale and swollen.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Seasonal itchy rhinorrhoea with eye symptoms in an atopic patient is allergic rhinitis.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a recurrent nasal problem.
Seasonal, itchy, eye involvement, atopic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Allergic rhinitis.**

elim: Facial pain and purulent discharge; not seasonal.
Lasts about a week; does not recur every spring.
Constant blockage and anosmia.
Non-allergic, triggered by temperature or smells, without itch.

steps.x: **B. Allergic rhinitis.** Itch + seasonal + atopy = allergic.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman develops itchy, raised red wheals over her trunk and arms 20 minutes after eating prawns. She has no lip or tongue swelling, wheeze or dizziness. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Wheals soon after shellfish without airway, breathing or circulation compromise is acute urticaria. Anaphylaxis needs ABC involvement.

steps.x: Diagnosis: is it a skin-only reaction or a systemic emergency?

clues: no lip or tongue swelling, wheeze or dizziness
steps.x: Immediate IgE skin reaction to shellfish with normal observations and no ABC compromise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute urticaria**.

elim: Delayed rash at a contact site, not wheals after food.
Needs airway, breathing or circulation compromise; she has none.
Target lesions, often after HSV or drugs.
Swelling without urticaria, not food-triggered.

steps.x: **A. Acute urticaria.** Hives without ABC problems = urticaria; with ABC problems = anaphylaxis.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has an itchy, red, blistering rash on her earlobes and under her watch strap. It began 2 days after she started wearing new costume jewellery. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. She has no urticaria elsewhere.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A delayed itchy rash confined to sites of contact with jewellery is allergic contact dermatitis (Type IV). Urticaria appears within minutes.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a rash with a clear pattern.

clues: earlobes and under her watch strap
steps.x: Delayed reaction exactly where metal touches skin: nickel allergy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Allergic contact dermatitis** (Type IV, nickel).

elim: Flexural and long-standing, not confined to metal contact sites.
Hot, tender, spreading, often febrile; not bilateral at jewellery sites.
Due to direct damage (soaps, water), not small metal contact.
Transient wheals within minutes, not a delayed blistering rash.

steps.x: **A. Allergic contact dermatitis.** Contact site + delayed = allergic contact dermatitis.

practice.stem: A 4 month old boy has had vomiting after feeds, loose stools with mucus, eczema and poor weight gain since he was switched from breast milk to formula at 2 months. He has no urticaria or swelling. His weight has fallen from the 50th to the 9th centile.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Delayed gut and skin symptoms with faltering growth after starting formula suggest non-IgE CMPA. IgE-mediated allergy gives urticaria or swelling within minutes.

steps.x: Diagnosis in an infant with symptoms tied to a change of feed.

clues: switched from breast milk to formula
steps.x: Multi-system delayed symptoms after formula introduction, faltering growth, no immediate IgE features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Non-IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy.**

elim: Needs gluten in the diet; he is 4 months old on milk only.
Does not explain mucus stools, eczema and the link to formula.
Would cause urticaria or swelling within minutes.
Projectile vomiting at 2 to 8 weeks, no diarrhoea or eczema.

steps.x: **D. Non-IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy.** After formula + multi-system + delayed = non-IgE CMPA.

practice.stem: A 35 year old man has had a constantly blocked nose for 3 months. He has used oxymetazoline spray several times a day since a cold 4 months ago, and it now works for only an hour. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. The nasal mucosa is red and swollen.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
practice.e: Prolonged oxymetazoline causes tachyphylaxis and rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa). Allergic rhinitis would be itchy with pale mucosa.

steps.x: It asks for a cause: what links the timeline to the spray?

clues: oxymetazoline spray several times a day
steps.x: Prolonged decongestant use with shrinking benefit (tachyphylaxis) and rebound congestion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Rhinitis medicamentosa** from the decongestant.

elim: Itch, sneezing and seasonal or allergen triggers, with pale mucosa.
Facial pain and purulent discharge.
Fixed, usually one-sided obstruction that a spray would not relieve at all.
Pale grape-like masses and loss of smell.

steps.x: **E. Rhinitis medicamentosa.** Weeks of decongestant + rebound = rhinitis medicamentosa.

practice.stem: A 10 month old girl develops urticaria around her mouth, lip swelling and vomiting 10 minutes after her first taste of cow's milk yoghurt. She has eczema. Her pulse rate is 130 bpm, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. There is no wheeze or stridor. BP is normal for age.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Urticaria and lip swelling within minutes of milk is IgE-mediated cow's milk allergy. Non-IgE allergy is delayed and lacks urticaria.

steps.x: Diagnosis: timing after the trigger separates IgE from non-IgE.
Immediate urticaria and angioedema after milk in an atopic infant, no ABC compromise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IgE-mediated cow's milk allergy.**

elim: No fever or contacts and onset 10 minutes after milk.
Bloating and diarrhoea, not urticaria and swelling.
Delayed onset (hours to days) without urticaria.
Fever and generalised rash, not 10 minutes after food.

steps.x: **B. IgE-mediated cow's milk allergy.** Minutes + urticaria/angioedema = IgE-mediated.

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman has had sneezing and itchy eyes every summer since her teens. She wants to know what she is allergic to. She is not taking antihistamines at present. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Skin prick testing with water and histamine controls identifies the IgE allergen. Total IgE is non-specific; patch testing is for contact dermatitis.

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation for suspected IgE allergy.
Seasonal IgE-mediated rhinitis; she is off antihistamines so the test will be valid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Skin prick testing** with controls.

elim: Confirms anaphylaxis after a severe reaction.
For infection, not allergy.
For delayed Type IV contact dermatitis.
Raised in atopy but does not identify the allergen.

steps.x: **D. Skin prick testing.** Immediate allergy = skin prick (or specific IgE).

practice.stem: A 26 year old dental nurse has a red, itchy, cracked rash on both hands that appears a day or two after long shifts wearing rubber gloves. She has never had hives, lip swelling or wheeze. Her temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 74 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Delayed hand dermatitis under gloves is allergic contact dermatitis, diagnosed by skin patch testing. Prick tests and RAST detect immediate IgE allergy.

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation: immediate or delayed allergy?

clues: never had hives, lip swelling or wheeze
steps.x: Delayed contact rash from rubber chemicals: Type IV.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Skin patch testing**, read after 2 to 3 days.

elim: Tests immediate IgE latex allergy, which she lacks.
For anaphylaxis.
Does not identify the allergen.
For immediate Type I latex allergy.

steps.x: **D. Skin patch testing.** Delayed contact = patch test.

practice.stem: A 21 year old student has sneezing and a runny nose on high pollen days. Symptoms do not affect her sleep, studies or sport. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg. She has not tried any treatment.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Mild allergic rhinitis not interfering with sleep or activities is treated first with oral loratadine. Intranasal steroids are for moderate to severe symptoms.

steps.x: Initial management: grade the severity.

clues: do not affect her sleep, studies or sport
steps.x: Mild intermittent allergic rhinitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral loratadine** (non-sedating antihistamine) plus allergen avoidance.

elim: For persistent symptoms after an intranasal steroid trial.
For moderate to severe symptoms.
Not for mild rhinitis.
Risks rhinitis medicamentosa.

steps.x: **C. Oral loratadine.** Mild = oral loratadine.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man has allergic rhinitis that disturbs his sleep. He has used intranasal mometasone correctly every day for 4 weeks with only partial improvement. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Oral loratadine instead of the spray
practice.e: If symptoms persist after 2 to 4 weeks of intranasal steroid, switch to fluticasone-azelastine. Long-term decongestants cause rhinitis medicamentosa.

steps.x: Next step after an intranasal steroid trial.
Moderate to severe rhinitis not controlled after a 2 to 4 week intranasal steroid trial.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Switch to **combined intranasal steroid and antihistamine** (fluticasone-azelastine).

elim: Causes tachyphylaxis and rhinitis medicamentosa.
A step down, not up.
For a structural deviation, not allergy.
He remains symptomatic.

steps.x: **B. Intranasal fluticasone-azelastine.** Steroid spray failed after 2 to 4 weeks → combination spray.

practice.stem: A 3 month old formula-fed boy has non-IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy with mild eczema, loose stools and reflux. He is gaining weight along the 25th centile. His pulse rate is 140 bpm and he is alert and well hydrated.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Mild to moderate formula-fed CMPA is managed with extensively hydrolysed formula. Goat's milk cross-reacts and lactose-free formula still contains milk protein.

steps.x: Initial management of mild to moderate formula-fed CMPA.
Mild to moderate non-IgE CMPA, growing well, formula-fed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Extensively hydrolysed formula** for a 2 to 6 week elimination trial.

elim: For severe cases or failure of hydrolysed formula.
Cross-reacts with cow's milk protein.
Still contains cow's milk protein.
Not first line under 6 months.

steps.x: **B. Extensively hydrolysed formula.** Mild to moderate CMPA = extensively hydrolysed formula.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has a patch test to investigate a rash under her watch strap. The test sites are covered for 48 hours and read at 72 hours, when the nickel site shows an itchy, red, raised reaction. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 120/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this delayed reaction?
practice.e: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV, T-cell-mediated reaction, which is why patch tests are read after 2 to 3 days.

steps.x: Mechanism: the delay is the clue.
A reaction days later at the contact site.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Type IV** delayed hypersensitivity: sensitised **T cells** recruit inflammation.

elim: Type II.
Type I gives a wheal within 15 minutes.
Type III, e.g. serum sickness.
Irritant reactions are not immune-mediated and do not need sensitisation.

steps.x: **E. Sensitised T-cell-mediated inflammation.** Days = T cells = Type IV.

glossary.Allergen: A normally harmless substance, such as pollen or milk protein, that triggers an allergic reaction.
glossary.Atopy: An inherited tendency to make IgE to allergens, causing eczema, asthma and hay fever.
glossary.IgE: Immunoglobulin E, the antibody that binds mast cells and drives immediate allergic reactions.
glossary.Mast cell: Tissue immune cell packed with histamine granules that releases them when IgE is cross-linked.
glossary.Basophil: A blood white cell similar to a mast cell, which also carries IgE and releases histamine.
glossary.Histamine: Mediator released by mast cells that causes itch, vasodilation, leaky vessels and smooth muscle contraction.
glossary.Degranulation: Release of stored chemicals, such as histamine, from mast cell or basophil granules.
glossary.Type I hypersensitivity: Immediate, IgE-mediated allergic reaction within minutes, e.g. hay fever, urticaria, anaphylaxis.
glossary.Type IV hypersensitivity: Delayed, T-cell-mediated reaction taking 2 to 3 days, e.g. allergic contact dermatitis.
glossary.Urticaria: Itchy, raised red wheals (hives) caused by histamine release in the skin.
glossary.Angioedema: Swelling of deeper skin layers, often lips, tongue or eyelids.
glossary.Allergic rhinitis: IgE-mediated inflammation of the nasal lining causing sneezing, itch and a runny, blocked nose.
glossary.Conjunctival: Relating to the conjunctiva, the thin membrane covering the white of the eye.
glossary.Allergic contact dermatitis: Delayed itchy rash where skin touched an allergen such as nickel, latex or hair dye.
glossary.Skin prick testing: Allergen drops pricked into forearm skin; a wheal at 15 minutes shows IgE sensitisation.
glossary.Skin patch testing: Allergens taped to the back and read after 2 to 3 days to diagnose contact dermatitis.
glossary.Specific IgE: IgE directed against one named allergen, measured in blood (RAST).
glossary.Wheal-and-flare: A raised swelling with surrounding redness, the immediate IgE skin reaction.
glossary.Mast cell tryptase: Enzyme released by mast cells; a raised level confirms anaphylaxis has occurred.
glossary.Anaphylaxis: Severe, life-threatening systemic allergic reaction with airway, breathing or circulation compromise.
glossary.CMPA: Cow's milk protein allergy: an immune reaction to the proteins in cow's milk.
glossary.Cow's milk protein allergy: Immune reaction in infants to cow's milk proteins, either IgE or non-IgE mediated.
glossary.Non-IgE-mediated: An allergy driven by T cells rather than IgE, with delayed symptoms and negative IgE tests.
glossary.Extensively hydrolysed formula: Infant formula with milk proteins broken into small fragments, first line for CMPA.
glossary.Milk ladder: A stepwise plan to reintroduce milk, starting with well-baked forms, after 6 months.
glossary.Faltering growth: Weight gain slower than expected, crossing down centile lines.
glossary.Loratadine: A non-sedating oral antihistamine; first line for mild allergic rhinitis.
glossary.Antihistamines: Drugs that block histamine H1 receptors to relieve itch, sneezing and hives.
glossary.Mometasone: An intranasal corticosteroid used for moderate to severe allergic rhinitis.
glossary.Fluticasone: A corticosteroid used as a nasal spray for allergic rhinitis.
glossary.Fluticasone-azelastine: Combined steroid and antihistamine nasal spray for rhinitis not controlled by a steroid spray.
glossary.Intranasal corticosteroid: A steroid nasal spray that reduces nasal inflammation over days.
glossary.Oxymetazoline: An alpha-agonist decongestant nasal spray; long-term use causes rebound congestion.
glossary.Decongestant: A drug that narrows nasal blood vessels to unblock the nose.
glossary.Tachyphylaxis: A rapidly falling response to a drug with repeated doses.
glossary.Rhinitis medicamentosa: Rebound nasal congestion caused by overuse of decongestant sprays.
glossary.Sensitisation: Making IgE to an allergen after first exposure, so later exposure triggers a reaction.
glossary.Adrenaline: Emergency drug for anaphylaxis, given intramuscularly into the thigh.
glossary.iMAP: International Milk Allergy in Primary care guideline for diagnosing and managing milk allergy in infants.
